posts.title: Why the broth goes on at half past five
posts.excerpt: At half past five each morning, head of broth Daniel Cho begins the slow simmering of our four signature broths long before our dining room doors open.
posts.content:
At half past five in the morning, Harbour Row is entirely dark. The streetlamps along the waterfront cast a cold amber glow across the wet pavement, and the first trams will not run for another hour. Inside number 14, Daniel Cho turns the brass key in the lock, hangs his coat near the entrance desk, and walks through the dark dining room into the kitchen. The eighteen tables are laid and waiting, their table burners cold beneath the copper pendants. In the kitchen, the work begins in silence before the town wakes up.

The four broths at Kosame cannot be hurried. Hot pot is often thought of as an evening meal, loud and companionable, but its true foundation is built in these early morning hours. By the time our doors open at seventeen hundred, each broth must possess a clear, settled depth that can simmer at a guest's table for two full hours without turning bitter or muddy. Achieving that balance requires steady heat and continuous attention long before the first guest steps across our threshold.

The morning starts with the pots that demand the longest extraction. Our white pork bone broth has already been simmering gently through the night, having started twelve hours earlier after the previous evening's close. Daniel checks its steady roll, skimming the surface with a fine wire ladle until the broth reaches its characteristic milky emulsion. Next, the large stockpot for our clear broth is filled with fresh cold water, whole chicken, and thick strips of dried kelp. This broth will simmer steadily for six hours, yielding a clean, golden stock that anchors half of nearly every split pot we serve.

At seven thirty, the morning market delivery arrives at the back door. Kwame Mensah unloads wooden crates of napa cabbage, dark winter greens, and firm tofu alongside cartons of dried shiitake and enoki mushrooms. The mushrooms and kelp go directly into the third pot for our forest broth, an earthy, entirely vegetarian preparation that simmers for three hours. Shortly after, Daniel heats rendered beef fat in a wide pan with dried chillies, garlic, and fragrant Sichuan peppers to build the fiery, aromatic base of our red broth, which simmers for four hours until it turns a deep, glowing brick red.

By ten in the morning, Inés Valero joins the kitchen to begin slicing sirloin, chuck, and pork belly on the cold counter. Meanwhile, Daniel monitors each simmering pot, adjusting the flames so the surface barely shivers. We do not use commercial bases, powders, or artificial thickeners. When a guest sits at an individual table burner and watches the steam rise from their split pot, they are tasting broths finished at dawn from whole bones, fresh market produce, and honest time.

By sixteen thirty, Tomás Ferreira is on the floor testing every burner and placing the polished steel pots on the tables. Aisha Rahman is at the booking desk confirming the evening's final reservations. When Mara Lindqvist unlocks the front doors at five o'clock, the dining room fills with warm light and the soft aroma of simmering stock. The long morning in the kitchen is complete, and the evening service begins exactly as it has since 2016.

posts.title: Clear or red: how to split your pot
posts.excerpt: Any two of the four broths share one split pot at no extra cost. A short guide to pairing them.
posts.content:
Clear is light and golden; red carries beef fat, dried chilli and Sichuan pepper. Many tables start with one of each and move vegetables to the clear side when the red turns hot.

White and forest pair well with either. Ask your server and we will set the pot before you sit.

posts.title: Booking a room for twelve
posts.excerpt: Room Three seats ten to fourteen on one long table. How far ahead to ask and what to tell us.
posts.content:
Room Three seats ten to fourteen guests along a single long table with three pots. Request it at least three days ahead through the Book a table button.

Tell us the date, the time, how many are coming and any dietary notes. We confirm by email within three hours during desk hours.
